sections.title: One job runs to completion
sections.body: JavaScript executes the current job on a call stack. A function call adds a frame and returning removes it. A job runs to completion before another queued job begins, so a long calculation blocks clicks, painting, and other queued work on that agent.

sections.title: Queues decide what runs next
sections.body: Timer callbacks and many events become tasks. Promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks become microtasks. After the current stack finishes, the runtime drains microtasks before taking the next task, which is why resolved promise callbacks normally run before a zero-delay timer.

sections.title: Timers schedule callbacks
sections.body: setTimeout(callback, 0) does not call the function immediately; it schedules a future task after the current job and earlier queued work. The delay is a minimum and may be longer because the thread is busy or the browser throttles timers. Store the timer ID when cancellation may be needed.

sections.title: Keep the main thread available
sections.body: Rendering and user input need opportunities to run. Split expensive work, avoid blocking loops, and clean up timers or subscriptions when UI ownership ends. React batching and effects add framework rules, but they still operate on JavaScript’s scheduling model.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Event loop and timers is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain event loop and timers to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Explain the call stack and run-to-completion. Distinguish tasks and microtasks. Treat a delay as a minimum, not an appointment. Connect scheduling to responsive interfaces.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using event loop and timers behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can event loop and timers affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using event loop and timers produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
